title: Japanese Mythology: Figures, Relationships and Story Cycles
description: The kami of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki mapped as a relationship graph: Izanagi and Izanami, Amaterasu in the cave, Susanoo and the eight-headed serpent, the descent of the imperial line, and the yokai of the folk tradition.
sources: The Kojiki, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)
Nihongi, translated by W. G. Aston (1896)
F. Hadland Davis, Myths and Legends of Japan (1912)
W. G. Aston, Shinto: The Way of the Gods (1905)
Yei Theodora Ozaki, Japanese Fairy Tales (1908)
portraitNote: Portraits are original illustrations in a single uniform style for the whole pack, stored locally in the portraits/japanese/ folder. No images are fetched from the network.

kojiki.t: The Kojiki, Records of Ancient Matters

hearn.t: Kwaidan: Stories and Studies of Strange Things

aston.t: Shinto: The Way of the Gods

profile.cosmicNature: Continuous, with no beginning made and no ending foretold. The first kami do not create the world - they 'come into being' in it, spontaneously, and then hide themselves. There is no creation from nothing, no cosmic war, and strikingly no eschatology at all: nothing in the tradition says the world will end. Time simply continues, and the imperial line continues with it.
profile.natureOfDivinity: Immanent and innumerable. Kami is not a class of powerful beings but a quality: anything that inspires awe can be kami - a mountain, an old tree, a waterfall, a remarkable person, an ancestor, a fox. They are conventionally counted as yaoyorozu, eight million, meaning uncountable. They are local before they are cosmic, and a shrine is usually to the kami of that specific place rather than to a universal god.
profile.afterlife: Yomi, the land of the dead, is not a punishment and has no judge. It is simply polluted - Izanami eats its food and cannot return, and Izanagi's visit leaves him needing a bath rather than absolution. Buddhist afterlives with judgment and rebirth were layered on from the sixth century and now do most of the funerary work, which is why Japanese funerals are overwhelmingly Buddhist while weddings and births are Shinto.
profile.systemMechanism: Purity against pollution, not good against evil. Kegare - the defilement of death, blood, sickness and disorder - is the problem, and the answer is ritual cleansing rather than repentance: misogi with water, harae with a wand. Susanoo is not punished for wickedness but expelled for pollution. Alongside this runs the political mechanism the chronicles were written to establish: the emperor descends from Amaterasu.
profile.canonTexts: The Kojiki (712) and the Nihon Shoki (720), both court compilations; the provincial Fudoki; the Engishiki's ritual prayers; and, for the folk stream, Edo-period yokai compendia and the collections of Hearn and others.

hierarchy.title: The Kami Who Came Into Being
hierarchy.blurb: Nothing is made from nothing. The first kami simply come into being when heaven and earth begin, and then hide themselves and do nothing further. Seven generations pass before anyone acts.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Izanagi washes the pollution of Yomi away, and the great kami come from the washing

hierarchy.title: The Three Noble Children
hierarchy.blurb: The sun from the left eye, the moon from the right, the storm from the nose. The sun is the elder sister and the moon her brother, which inverts the arrangement of most traditions.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: The sun hides in a cave, and the world has to be got back

hierarchy.title: The Plain of High Heaven
hierarchy.blurb: Heaven works by assembly. Eight hundred kami gather in a dry riverbed, refer the problem to the kami of counsel, and act on his plan - which turns out to involve a mirror, a rooster and an indecent dance.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Heaven sends its grandchild down to rule the land below

hierarchy.title: The Descent and the Line
hierarchy.blurb: Ninigi comes down with mirror, jewel and sword, chooses blossom over rock and so makes human life short, and four generations later his descendant takes Yamato. This is what the chronicles were written to establish.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Beneath the court myth: the kami people actually pray to, and the buddhas who arrived

hierarchy.title: Kami of Daily Life, and the Arrivals
hierarchy.blurb: Inari has a third of all the shrines in Japan. Kannon, Jizo, Benzaiten and Daikokuten came from India by way of China and stayed, and for a thousand years kami and buddha were identified with one another.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: And a separate stream: what is in the mountains, the rivers and the snow

hierarchy.title: The Folk Stream
hierarchy.blurb: The yokai are not part of the court mythology and mostly reach us in Edo-period form. They encode practical warnings - the river that drowns children, the mountain that kills in winter - and a great deal of comedy.

entities.name: Amenominakanushi
entities.role: The first kami, who came into being and hid
epithets: Lord of the August Centre of Heaven
entities.abode: The Plain of High Heaven, then hidden
entities.bio: The first kami to come into being at the start of heaven and earth, who immediately concealed himself and did nothing further.
entities.longBio: The Kojiki opens by saying that when heaven and earth began, three kami came into being in the Plain of High Heaven, of whom Amenominakanushi was first - and then that all three hid themselves. That is the entire account. He does not create, command, father anyone or reappear. This is one of the most distinctive things about the Japanese tradition: it does not begin with a maker. Things come into being, and the first ones to do so promptly withdraw, leaving the work to later generations. Seven generations of kami follow before Izanagi and Izanami do anything at all. Later Shinto theologians, particularly in the Edo period and under some Meiji influence, tried to promote him into a supreme creator god, which the text gives them very little to work with.
entities.variantTraditions: The elevation of Amenominakanushi to a supreme deity is a much later theological project, not a reading the Kojiki supports.

entities.name: Izanagi
entities.role: He Who Invites; father of the islands and of the great kami
domains: the fathering of the three noble children
entities.abode: Awaji, and afterwards a hidden palace
entities.bio: With Izanami he stirred the sea into the first island, and after her death he fathered Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi and Susanoo by washing.
entities.longBio: Izanagi and Izanami stand on the floating bridge of heaven and stir the brine below with a jewelled spear; the drops that fall from its tip make the first island. They descend, marry, and produce the islands of Japan and a great many kami. Their first attempt fails because Izanami spoke first in the marriage ritual - which the chronicles present as an error to be corrected, and which is one of several places where the text's politics show. Izanami dies giving birth to fire. Izanagi follows her into Yomi, is horrified by what he finds, and flees. Then, washing the pollution off in a river, he produces his most important children from the act of cleaning himself: Amaterasu from his left eye, Tsukuyomi from his right, and Susanoo from his nose.
entities.variantTraditions: The Nihon Shoki gives several alternative versions of nearly every episode side by side, prefaced 'in one writing it is said', which is unusual candour for a chronicle.

entities.name: Izanami
entities.role: She Who Invites; mother of the islands, and of death
entities.abode: Yomi, the land of the dead
entities.bio: She bore the islands and died bearing fire; when her husband saw her decayed in Yomi she pursued him and became death itself.
entities.longBio: Izanami bears the islands and the kami, and is fatally burned giving birth to Kagutsuchi, fire. Izanagi goes down to Yomi to bring her back. She says she has already eaten the food of that place but will ask its powers, and asks him not to look at her. He waits, grows impatient, breaks a tooth from his comb for a torch, and sees her rotting and full of maggots. Shamed and enraged, she sends the hags of Yomi after him, and he escapes by throwing down his headdress and comb, which become grapes and bamboo shoots, and finally peaches. At the pass they part with the exchange that establishes mortality: she promises to strangle a thousand people a day, and he answers that he will cause fifteen hundred to be born.
entities.variantTraditions: The Yomi descent has clear structural parallels with Orpheus and with Persephone, and the parallels are usually treated as typological rather than as evidence of contact.

entities.name: Kagutsuchi
entities.role: The fire whose birth killed his mother
symbols: the ten-span sword that killed him
entities.abode: Cut into eight pieces, each a mountain
entities.bio: His birth burned Izanami to death, and his father cut him apart in grief, each piece becoming a mountain kami.
entities.longBio: Kagutsuchi is the last child Izanami bears and the one that kills her, burning her as he is born. Izanagi, weeping, takes his ten-span sword and cuts off the infant's head, and from the blood on the blade, the blood dripping from the rocks, and the eight severed pieces of the body come a further set of kami - including Takemikazuchi the thunder-sword and the mountain kami. The episode is characteristic of the Kojiki's method: every act of violence is also a genealogy, and the world fills up with kami as a by-product of grief and anger. Fire kami are treated seriously in practice, since Japanese towns were built of wood and paper, and shrines to fire-quelling kami are common.
entities.variantTraditions: Kagutsuchi is called Homusubi in the Nihon Shoki, one of many places where the two chronicles differ in name.

entities.name: Amaterasu
entities.role: The sun goddess, ancestor of the imperial line
epithets: Ruler of the Plain of High Heaven
entities.abode: The Plain of High Heaven; her shrine at Ise
festivals: The Kannamesai and Niinamesai rice offerings
the Ise Shikinen Sengu rebuilding every twenty years
entities.worship: The Grand Shrine at Ise is her seat and the most sacred site in Shinto; it has been demolished and rebuilt on an adjacent plot every twenty years for over a millennium.
entities.bio: Born from Izanagi's left eye; she withdrew into a cave and had to be lured out, and her descendants rule Japan.
entities.longBio: Amaterasu is the most important kami and, unusually among world traditions, the sun is female and the moon her brother. She rules the Plain of High Heaven and tends its rice fields and weaving hall. Her brother Susanoo's escalating outrages - breaking the paddy dykes, defiling her hall, and finally flinging a flayed horse through the roof of the weaving room so that a weaver is killed - drive her into the rock cave of heaven, and the world goes dark. The kami gather outside and lure her out with a mirror, a rooster and Ame-no-Uzume's dance. Her grandson Ninigi is sent down to rule the land, carrying the mirror, jewel and sword that are still the imperial regalia, and from him the imperial house descends.
entities.variantTraditions: The chronicles were compiled to establish exactly that descent, and Amaterasu's supremacy over other kami may owe as much to the political programme as to older belief.

entities.name: Tsukuyomi
entities.role: The moon, who killed the food goddess and lost his sister
entities.abode: The realm of night, apart from his sister
entities.bio: Born from Izanagi's right eye; he killed Ukemochi over a meal and Amaterasu never looked at him again.
entities.longBio: Tsukuyomi is the least developed of the three noble children and has one significant story. Sent by Amaterasu to visit the food goddess Ukemochi, he is served a feast she produces from her own mouth and body - rice from her mouth, fish from the sea, game from the land. Disgusted at being offered what he sees as filth, he kills her. From her corpse come the crops: millet from her forehead, rice from her belly, wheat and beans from other parts, and the silkworm from her eyebrows. Amaterasu, told what he has done, declares him a wicked deity and refuses to look at him ever again - and that is why the sun and moon are never in the sky together. It is a small, cold story, and it is nearly all he has.
entities.variantTraditions: The Kojiki attributes the killing of the food goddess to Susanoo instead, and calls her Ogetsuhime; the Nihon Shoki gives it to Tsukuyomi.

entities.name: Susanoo
entities.role: Storm god, exile, and dragon-slayer
symbols: the Kusanagi sword taken from the serpent's tail
entities.abode: Izumo, after his expulsion from heaven
entities.worship: Yasaka Shrine in Kyoto and the Izumo shrines are his principal seats; the Gion Festival is associated with him as a warder-off of plague.
entities.bio: Expelled from heaven for pollution, he descended to Izumo, killed the eight-headed serpent, and became a founder rather than a villain.
entities.longBio: Susanoo is born from Izanagi's nose and refuses his assignment, weeping until the mountains wither because he wants to go to his mother in Yomi. Sent to say goodbye to Amaterasu, he behaves so badly in heaven - breaking the rice dykes, fouling the hall, throwing a flayed horse into the weaving room - that she hides in a cave and he is expelled, his beard cut and his nails pulled out. Then the character turns completely. In Izumo he finds an old couple weeping over the last of their eight daughters, due to be eaten by the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi. He gets the serpent drunk on eight vats of sake, cuts it apart, finds a sword in its tail, marries the girl, and composes the first Japanese poem. He is not redeemed; he was always both.
entities.variantTraditions: The Izumo material may preserve a rival tradition to the Yamato court's, and Susanoo's demotion in heaven and prominence in Izumo has been read politically.

entities.name: Ame-no-Uzume
entities.role: Who danced the sun out of the cave
entities.abode: The Plain of High Heaven
entities.bio: She danced on an overturned tub outside the cave until the assembled kami laughed loud enough to make Amaterasu curious.
entities.longBio: With the sun hidden and the world dark, eight hundred kami gather at the cave and try everything. What works is Ame-no-Uzume. She binds up her sleeves with vine, takes bamboo grass in her hand, sets an empty tub upside down before the cave, and dances on it, stamping until it booms, and in her ecstasy pulls down her dress. The eight hundred kami roar with laughter. Amaterasu, who cannot imagine what there is to laugh about in a dark world, slides the rock door open a crack to ask - and is shown her own face in a mirror held up as another and greater deity, and drawn out while a rope is stretched behind her. She is also the one who faces down Sarutahiko on the road of the descent, by staring him out.
entities.variantTraditions: Uzume is the patron of kagura and of the performing arts generally, and the story is regularly read as the origin of ritual dance.

entities.name: Omoikane
entities.role: The kami of counsel who devised the plan
entities.abode: The dry bed of the river of heaven
entities.bio: When the sun hid, the eight hundred kami gathered and put the problem to him, and he designed the solution.
entities.longBio: Omoikane's name means something like the one who combines the thoughts of many, and his function is exactly that: when the kami assemble in the dry bed of the heavenly river with an emergency, they refer it to him and he produces a plan. For the cave he specifies the whole apparatus - long-crying birds to be made to crow, a mirror to be forged, jewels strung, a sakaki tree uprooted and hung with them, prayers, and Uzume's dance - and it works. He is consulted again over who should be sent down to pacify the land before Ninigi's descent. He is a rare thing in mythology: a deity of committee work who is genuinely good at it, and whose contribution is procedure rather than power.
entities.variantTraditions: Omoikane is a son of Takamimusubi, one of the three original hidden kami, which quietly gives the planning function a very old pedigree.

entities.name: Takemikazuchi
entities.role: The thunder-sword who won the land by an arm-wrestle
symbols: the sword set upright on a wave
the catfish held down by a rock
entities.abode: Kashima Shrine
entities.bio: Born from the blood on the sword that killed the fire kami, he sat on a sword-point and won Japan in the first sumo match.
entities.longBio: Takemikazuchi comes into being from the blood on Izanagi's blade after the killing of Kagutsuchi. When heaven decides the land below must be handed over before Ninigi descends, he is sent with another kami; they plant a sword upright on the crest of a wave and sit cross-legged on its point to make their demand. Okuninushi refers them to his sons. One agrees; the other, Takeminakata, seizes Takemikazuchi's hand, which turns into an icicle and then a sword blade, and is crushed and thrown - the encounter is traditionally regarded as the first sumo bout. Takemikazuchi is also credited with pinning down the giant catfish whose movements cause earthquakes, with a foundation stone at Kashima.
entities.variantTraditions: The earthquake-catfish association is Edo-period and produced a whole genre of popular prints after the 1855 Ansei quake.

entities.name: Sarutahiko
entities.role: The crossroads kami who guided the descent
domains: the meeting of heaven and earth
entities.abode: Ise, at the crossing of the eight roads
entities.bio: A huge red-faced kami who blocked the road of the descent and became its guide, and married the dancer who faced him.
entities.longBio: As Ninigi's party comes down, they find the way blocked by an enormous kami standing at the eight crossroads of heaven, seven spans tall with a nose seven hands long, a red face and eyes that glow like mirrors. Nobody dares approach him except Ame-no-Uzume, who is sent because, the text says, she can outface anyone; she bares her breast and stares him down and asks who he is. He turns out to be entirely friendly - he has come to offer himself as a guide. He leads the party to earth, and afterwards marries Uzume. His appearance later shaped the standard image of the tengu, and he is regarded as a patron of martial arts and of safe travel.
entities.variantTraditions: The physical description of Sarutahiko is widely thought to have fed into the long-nosed tengu of later folklore.

entities.name: Ninigi
entities.role: The grandson sent down to rule the land
domains: the founding of the imperial line
entities.abode: Takachiho in Hyuga
entities.bio: Amaterasu sent him down with mirror, jewel and sword to rule the islands, and he chose the wrong bride.
entities.longBio: Ninigi is sent down from heaven to rule the land, carrying the three items - the mirror Yata no Kagami, the jewel Yasakani no Magatama and the sword Kusanagi - that remain the Japanese imperial regalia to this day. He descends on Mount Takachiho with an escort of kami. Offered the two daughters of the mountain kami, he takes the beautiful Konohanasakuya and sends back her elder sister Iwanaga, Rock-Long, who is ugly. Their father explains what he has thrown away: had he kept Iwanaga, his descendants' lives would have been enduring as rock; taking only Konohanasakuya, they will be brilliant and brief as blossom. That is the Japanese account of why emperors, and people, die.
entities.variantTraditions: The regalia are real objects in imperial custody; they are not displayed, and no reigning emperor is said to have seen the mirror.

entities.name: Konohanasakuya
entities.role: Blossom Princess; kami of Mount Fuji
entities.abode: Mount Fuji
entities.worship: The Sengen shrines around and on Mount Fuji are hers; climbers have long prayed at them.
entities.bio: Ninigi's bride, who proved her fidelity by giving birth in a burning hut, and whose choosing made human life short.
entities.longBio: Konohanasakuya is chosen by Ninigi over her elder sister, and the choice is why life is short and lovely rather than long and dull. She conceives after a single night, and Ninigi doubts the child is his. Her answer is not argument but ordeal: she builds a doorless hut, seals herself inside, sets it alight, and declares that if the child is a heavenly grandchild's it will come to no harm. She gives birth to three sons in the fire, unharmed. She is the kami of Mount Fuji, and her shrines ring it; the volcano and the blossom belong to the same figure, which is a very precise piece of symbolism - both are beautiful, both are brief, and one of them will kill you.
entities.variantTraditions: Her identification with Fuji is somewhat later than the Kojiki, which does not make the connection explicitly.

entities.name: Iwanaga
entities.role: Rock-Long Princess, the sister sent back
entities.abode: The mountains
entities.bio: Ninigi returned her for being ugly, and with her went the enduring life she would have given his line.
entities.longBio: Iwanaga is offered to Ninigi alongside her sister by their father the mountain kami, and Ninigi sends her back because she is ugly. Her father's response is one of the sharpest passages in the Kojiki: he explains that he sent both deliberately, so that the heavenly grandchild's life would be enduring as rock through Iwanaga and flourishing as blossom through her sister, and that by keeping only one he has chosen a life that blooms and falls. From this, the text says, the lives of the emperors have been short - and by extension so are everyone's. Iwanaga herself is given almost nothing beyond her rejection, which makes the story bleaker: the thing that was refused does not get a voice.
entities.variantTraditions: Some later folk traditions give Iwanaga a more active role, cursing the shortness of human life rather than merely embodying the loss.

entities.name: Okuninushi
entities.role: Lord of the Great Land, who built the country and handed it over
entities.abode: Izumo
festivals: Kamiarizuki, when the kami of all Japan are said to gather at Izumo in the tenth month
entities.worship: Izumo Taisha is one of the oldest and most important shrines in Japan, and is visited particularly for matchmaking.
entities.bio: A younger son abused by eighty brothers who built up the land, then ceded it to heaven for a great shrine.
entities.longBio: Okuninushi begins as the put-upon youngest of eighty brothers, carrying their bags on a courtship journey. He stops to help a flayed hare his brothers have tormented, telling it to wash in fresh water and roll in cattail pollen; the hare, a kami in disguise, tells him he will win the princess instead of them. They kill him twice for it and he is revived twice. He escapes to the underworld, survives Susanoo's tests, steals his sword, bow and koto, and elopes with his daughter. Then he builds up the land - agriculture, medicine, fisheries. When heaven demands it for Ninigi, he agrees to hand it over on one condition: a shrine as tall as the palace of heaven. Izumo Taisha is that shrine.
entities.variantTraditions: The Izumo cycle sits oddly inside a Yamato court document, and is widely read as an incorporated rival tradition, its concession negotiated rather than forced.

entities.name: Inari
entities.role: Kami of rice, foxes, and prosperity
entities.abode: Fushimi Inari at Kyoto, and some thirty thousand other shrines
festivals: Hatsuuma, the first horse day of the second month
entities.worship: About thirty thousand shrines. Offerings of rice, sake and fried tofu, which foxes are said to favour; donated torii from businesses line the approaches.
entities.bio: The most widely enshrined kami in Japan, served by fox messengers, and of no fixed sex.
entities.longBio: Inari has more shrines than any other kami - around a third of all shrines in Japan - and is the clearest case of a deity defined by function rather than personality. Inari is rice, and therefore wealth, and therefore by extension commerce, industry, and the prosperity of any enterprise; merchants and companies dedicate torii, which is why the paths at Fushimi Inari run for miles under thousands of donated gates. Inari's sex is not fixed and varies by shrine and period - sometimes an old man carrying rice, sometimes a young woman, sometimes androgynous - and the tradition is untroubled by this. The white foxes at every shrine are messengers, not the kami, though popular usage constantly confuses the two.
entities.variantTraditions: Inari is identified with the Kojiki's Ukanomitama and, in Buddhist contexts, with Dakiniten, an imported figure; the identifications are layered rather than exclusive.

entities.name: Hachiman
entities.role: Kami of archery and war, and protector of Japan
entities.abode: Usa Shrine, and Iwashimizu at Kyoto
entities.worship: Roughly twenty-five thousand shrines, second only to Inari. Samurai families were closely attached to him, and archery rites remain part of his festivals.
entities.bio: A deified emperor who became the tutelary kami of the samurai, and the clearest case of Shinto and Buddhism fused.
entities.longBio: Hachiman is generally identified with the semi-legendary Emperor Ojin, deified, and he became the patron kami of the Minamoto clan and then of the warrior class as a whole - which made him one of the most politically consequential deities in Japanese history. He is also the sharpest illustration of shinbutsu-shugo, the fusion of Shinto and Buddhism: from the eighth century he was styled Hachiman Daibosatsu, Great Bodhisattva Hachiman, a kami holding Buddhist rank, and his shrines were staffed by Buddhist monks for a thousand years until the forced separation of 1868. His oracle at Usa was consulted on matters of state, including whether a monk should be permitted to take the throne.
entities.variantTraditions: The Meiji separation of Shinto and Buddhism dismantled a millennium of syncretism by decree; the pre-1868 Hachiman is not quite the same figure as the post-1868 one.

entities.name: Raijin and Fujin
entities.role: The gods of thunder and wind
entities.abode: The sky, and the gates of temples
entities.bio: A demon-faced drummer whose ring of taiko makes thunder, and a wind god carrying the storms in a bag.
entities.longBio: Raijin beats a ring of taiko drums that circles his back to make thunder, and Fujin carries the winds in an enormous bag over his shoulders; the two are usually shown together, one green and one red, wild-haired and demonic, and they flank temple gates as guardians. They belong to the class of kami that is closer to the frightening than the benevolent, and their imagery owes something to Buddhist iconography imported from the continent. A widespread folk belief holds that Raijin eats children's navels, which is why mothers tell children to cover their stomachs during a thunderstorm. Fujin's winds were credited with the storms that destroyed the Mongol invasion fleets in 1274 and 1281 - the kamikaze, the divine wind.
entities.variantTraditions: The Tawaraya Sotatsu screen of the two is among the most famous works of Japanese art; the pairing may descend from Greek models transmitted along the Silk Road.

entities.name: Ryujin
entities.role: Dragon king of the sea
entities.abode: Ryugu-jo, the palace under the sea
entities.bio: He holds the jewels that raise and lower the tide, and his coral palace is where time runs differently.
entities.longBio: Ryujin lives in Ryugu-jo, a palace of coral and crystal at the bottom of the sea where the four seasons occur simultaneously in four directions and where time passes at a different rate from the surface. He controls the tides with two jewels, the kanju and manju, which lower and raise the water, and lending them decides battles - the Empress Jingu is said to have used them against Korea. His daughter Otohime hosts Urashima Taro for what feels like three days and turns out to be three hundred years. Another daughter, Toyotama, marries a grandson of Ninigi and gives birth in her true dragon form after asking him not to look; he looks, and she leaves, which puts the same broken taboo in the imperial genealogy as in the Yomi story.
entities.variantTraditions: Ryujin, Watatsumi and Owatatsumi are variously the same figure or distinct sea kami depending on the text.

entities.name: Ebisu
entities.role: The laughing god of fishermen and fortune
symbols: the sea bream under one arm
entities.abode: The shore, and every shop counter
entities.bio: The only wholly Japanese member of the Seven Lucky Gods, identified with the deformed first child Izanagi and Izanami set adrift.
entities.longBio: Ebisu is one of the Seven Lucky Gods and the only one of native origin - the other six are Indian or Chinese imports, which by itself says a great deal about Japanese religion. He is shown fat, smiling, in court dress and a tall folded hat, carrying a fishing rod and a large sea bream. He is deaf, which is why his festival involves a good deal of noise to get his attention, and he does not hear the summons to Izumo in the tenth month, so he stays behind while the other kami are away. He is usually identified with Hiruko, the leech-child, Izanagi and Izanami's malformed firstborn who was set adrift in a reed boat - a discarded child who washed ashore and became the god of luck.
entities.variantTraditions: The Ebisu-Hiruko identification is not in the Kojiki and developed much later; the Seven Lucky Gods as a set are a Muromachi-period assembly.

entities.name: Daikokuten
entities.role: God of wealth, with the mallet and the rice bales
entities.abode: The kitchen, and the storehouse
entities.bio: A ferocious Hindu destroyer imported through Buddhism and softened, in Japan, into a smiling god of the pantry.
entities.longBio: Daikokuten arrives in Japan as Mahakala, a wrathful form associated with Shiva and adopted as a Buddhist protector - a black, terrifying destroyer. In Japan he becomes a stout, grinning figure in a flat hood, standing on two bales of rice with a sack over his shoulder and a mallet that produces money when struck. The transformation is nearly total, and appears to have been helped by a pun: the characters for his name can also be read Okuninushi, so the imported figure merged with the Izumo land-builder. He is a god of the kitchen and the storehouse, and his image stood in temple kitchens and farmhouses. Rats are associated with him, being where the rice is.
entities.variantTraditions: The Mahakala-Daikokuten-Okuninushi chain is one of the most extreme transformations in the pack: a destroyer becomes a pantry god by way of a homophone.

entities.name: Benzaiten
entities.role: Goddess of music, eloquence and flowing things
entities.abode: Enoshima, Chikubushima and Itsukushima
entities.bio: The Indian Sarasvati, arrived through Buddhism, and the only woman among the Seven Lucky Gods.
entities.longBio: Benzaiten is the Japanese form of the Hindu river goddess Sarasvati, transmitted through Buddhist texts, and she keeps the essential character: everything that flows - water, music, speech, and by a natural extension knowledge and eventually money. She plays the biwa rather than the vina. Her shrines are almost always on islands or beside water, at Enoshima, Chikubushima and Itsukushima with its torii standing in the sea. A white serpent is her messenger, and a persistent folk belief holds that couples who visit her shrine together will be separated, because she is jealous - a piece of local colour with no basis in the doctrine. She is the only female member of the Seven Lucky Gods.
entities.variantTraditions: The comparison with the Hindu pack is direct: Benzaiten and Saraswati are the same goddess at two ends of a transmission, and the differences are instructive.

entities.name: Kannon
entities.role: Bodhisattva of compassion
epithets: She Who Perceives the Sounds of the World
entities.abode: Sensoji at Asakusa, and thirty-three pilgrimage temples
entities.bio: The Chinese Guanyin arrived in Japan and stayed, including among Christians who hid a cross behind her.
entities.longBio: Kannon is the Japanese form of Guanyin, and therefore of Avalokitesvara, and arrives already having changed sex once in China. The thirty-three-temple pilgrimage circuits dedicated to her are among the oldest and most walked in Japan, and Sensoji in Tokyo, founded on a Kannon image said to have been pulled from the river in a fisherman's net, is the country's most visited temple. Her most remarkable Japanese chapter is the Maria Kannon: during the two-and-a-half centuries when Christianity was banned, hidden Christian communities in Kyushu venerated images of Kannon holding a child, sometimes with a cross concealed on the back, as the Virgin Mary. The statues are indistinguishable from ordinary Kannon figures to an inspector.
entities.variantTraditions: The Maria Kannon statues survive in museums in Nagasaki and elsewhere and are among the most poignant objects in Japanese religious history.

entities.name: Jizo
entities.role: Guardian of travellers, and of dead children
epithets: Guardian of the Riverbank of Souls
domains: the rescue of souls from hell
entities.abode: Roadsides, crossroads, and the dry riverbed of Sai
entities.bio: Small stone figures at every roadside, dressed in red bibs by parents of dead children whose souls he shelters.
entities.longBio: Jizo is the most physically present figure in Japanese religion - small weathered stone statues stand at roadsides, crossroads, temple gates and mountain passes everywhere in the country. He vowed not to enter buddhahood until all beings are freed from hell, and he travels the realms of rebirth as a simple monk. His particular charge is children who die young, including stillbirths and miscarriages, who are said to be at Sai no Kawara, a dry riverbed, endlessly piling stones into towers that demons knock down; Jizo hides them in his sleeves and protects them. Bereaved parents dress his statues in red bibs and knitted caps and leave toys and pinwheels, and the sight of a row of them so dressed is unmistakable.
entities.variantTraditions: The mizuko kuyo rites for lost pregnancies are a modern development around Jizo and are the subject of considerable debate in Japan.

entities.name: Ukemochi
entities.role: The food goddess killed at her own banquet
entities.abode: Killed, and become the crops
entities.bio: She produced a feast from her own body, was killed for it in disgust, and her corpse became the staple crops.
entities.longBio: Sent a divine guest, Ukemochi turns to the land and produces boiled rice from her mouth, turns to the sea and produces fish, turns to the mountains and produces game, and sets it all out as a banquet. Her visitor - Tsukuyomi in the Nihon Shoki, Susanoo in the Kojiki, where she is called Ogetsuhime - is revolted at being offered food that came out of a body and kills her. Then from the corpse come the things that feed Japan: millet from the forehead, rice from the belly, wheat and beans from the genitals and rectum, and the silkworm from the eyebrows. It is a straightforward dema-deity story of the kind found across the Pacific, in which the staple crops come from a murdered body.
entities.variantTraditions: The two chronicles assign the killing to different gods, and the divergence is one of the clearest cases of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki simply disagreeing.

entities.name: Emperor Jimmu
entities.role: The first emperor, great-grandson of the heavenly grandchild
symbols: the bow with the golden kite
entities.abode: Yamato, after the eastward campaign
entities.bio: He marched east from Hyuga, was guided by a three-legged crow, and founded the imperial line in 660 BCE by tradition.
entities.longBio: Jimmu is the fourth generation from Ninigi and the point at which the chronicles cross from the age of the gods into the age of emperors, which is exactly what they were written to accomplish. He sets out east from Hyuga to find a place from which to govern, loses a brother to an arrow after fighting eastward into the sun and turning round to fight with the sun behind him instead, is saved when a sword is dropped through a storehouse roof by Takemikazuchi, and is guided over the mountains by Yatagarasu, a three-legged crow sent from heaven. He takes Yamato and is enthroned on a date traditionally given as 660 BCE. That date is a later calculation, and no historian treats Jimmu as a person.
entities.variantTraditions: The 660 BCE date derives from Chinese calendrical cycles applied retroactively; the Meiji state made it a national holiday, and the political use of Jimmu in the 1930s and 40s was considerable.

entities.name: Yamato Takeru
entities.role: The prince who conquered in a dress and died of a mountain
domains: the loneliness of the useful son
entities.abode: The eastern provinces, and a plain at Nobono
entities.bio: Feared by his own father and sent on endless campaigns, he killed by trickery and died from insulting a mountain kami.
entities.longBio: Yamato Takeru kills his elder brother for a slight, so casually that his father the emperor becomes frightened of him and sends him away on campaigns that are plainly meant to kill him. He kills the Kumaso chieftains by dressing as a girl and getting close enough to stab them, and the Izumo brave by proposing they exchange swords, having made himself a wooden one. His aunt at Ise gives him the sword Kusanagi from the serpent's tail, and it saves him when enemies fire a grass plain around him. His wife throws herself into the sea to calm it for him. Returning, he insults a mountain kami, is struck with a hailstorm and sickness, and dies on a plain, singing of Yamato. He becomes a white bird and flies away.
entities.variantTraditions: The Kojiki's Yamato Takeru is a considerably more melancholy figure than the Nihon Shoki's, and his lament for his homeland is among the best-known passages in Japanese literature.

entities.name: Momotaro
entities.role: The Peach Boy who went to Ogre Island
entities.abode: A village, and Onigashima
entities.bio: Found inside a peach by a childless couple, he took millet dumplings and three animals and cleared out the ogres.
entities.longBio: An old woman washing clothes at the river sees a giant peach come floating down; she takes it home, and when she and her husband cut it open a boy is inside. Grown, Momotaro announces he is going to Onigashima, Ogre Island, to deal with the oni who have been raiding the district, and asks his mother for kibi dango, millet dumplings. On the road he meets a dog, a monkey and a pheasant, and recruits each with half a dumpling. Together they cross to the island, defeat the oni, and come back with the treasure the ogres had stolen. It is the most universally known Japanese folk tale, taught to every child - and, precisely because of that, it was used heavily as propaganda during the Pacific War.
entities.variantTraditions: The wartime use of Momotaro, including animated films in which he leads an assault on enemy islands, is well documented and now uncomfortable.

entities.name: Urashima Taro
entities.role: The fisherman who lost three hundred years
domains: the box that must not be opened
entities.abode: Ryugu-jo, and then a village he does not recognise
entities.bio: He saved a turtle, spent three days in the sea-king's palace, returned to find three centuries gone, and opened the box.
entities.longBio: Urashima Taro rescues a turtle that children are tormenting on the beach. The turtle returns as a messenger of Ryujin and carries him to the dragon palace under the sea, where the princess Otohime entertains him and where the four seasons occur at once in four directions. After three days he grows homesick and asks to leave. She gives him a lacquered box, the tamatebako, and tells him never to open it. On shore, nothing is familiar; three hundred years have passed. Finding no one who remembers him and no house where his stood, he opens the box - and the white smoke that comes out is the years he was away, and he ages three centuries in an instant and dies, or becomes a crane.
entities.variantTraditions: A version appears in the Nihon Shoki and the Manyoshu, making this among the oldest attested tales in the pack; the endings vary considerably.

entities.name: Yamata no Orochi
entities.role: The eight-headed serpent of Izumo
domains: the annual tribute of a daughter
symbols: moss and trees on its back
entities.abode: The valleys of Izumo
entities.bio: A serpent with eight heads spanning eight valleys, killed by Susanoo with sake, and carrying Kusanagi in its tail.
entities.longBio: The serpent has eight heads and eight tails, eyes red as winter cherries, moss and cypress growing on its back, and a body spanning eight valleys and eight hills, and its belly is permanently raw and bleeding. It has eaten seven of an old couple's eight daughters, one a year, and is due to take the last. Susanoo's plan is unglamorous and effective: build a fence with eight gates, put a vat of strong sake behind each, and wait. Each head drinks from its own vat and the serpent falls asleep, and he cuts it into pieces. In the fourth tail he finds a sword, which he sends up to Amaterasu as a peace offering; it becomes Kusanagi, one of the three imperial regalia. The story is often read as a river being tamed.
entities.variantTraditions: The iron-working of Izumo and the red rivers of its smelting have been proposed as the serpent's origin; the reading is plausible and unproven.

entities.name: Kitsune
entities.role: The fox that gains a tail every century
symbols: the woman with a shadow that is a fox
entities.abode: Fields, shrines, and other people's houses
entities.bio: A fox grows a tail every hundred years and turns white or gold at nine, and may live as a woman for decades before being found out.
entities.longBio: Kitsune gain power with age: a tail per century, up to nine, at which point the fur turns white or gold and the fox can see and hear anything happening anywhere. They shapeshift, most often into women, and the fox-wife story is a fixed type - she marries a man, keeps house faithfully, bears children, and is exposed years later by a dog, a reflection, or a shadow that has a tail in it, whereupon she must leave. Some serve Inari and are benevolent messengers; others, the nogitsune, deceive and possess. Fox possession was a recognised diagnosis in Japan into the twentieth century, with families identified as fox-owning and shunned accordingly, which gave the folklore real social consequences.
entities.variantTraditions: The kitsune type is shared with Chinese huli jing and Korean kumiho; the Japanese Inari association is distinctive.

entities.name: Tengu
entities.role: The long-nosed mountain spirits who teach swordsmanship
entities.abode: The deep mountains, particularly Kurama and Mount Takao
entities.bio: Once bird-demons, later mountain ascetics who abduct the proud and teach swordsmanship to those they favour.
entities.longBio: Tengu begin as straightforwardly malevolent bird-demons who abduct people, set fires and possess women, and are particularly associated with arrogant Buddhist priests, who were said to be reborn as tengu for their pride. Over time they soften into something closer to dangerous mountain hermits with their own society, dressed as yamabushi ascetics, and two forms settle: the crow-headed karasu-tengu and the red-faced, enormously long-nosed daitengu, whose face probably descends from Sarutahiko. Their great legend is that Sojobo, king of the tengu of Mount Kurama, taught swordsmanship to the boy Minamoto no Yoshitsune, which is why Japan's most celebrated warrior fought as he did. They are proud, easily offended, and dangerous to mock.
entities.variantTraditions: The shift from demon to ambiguous teacher happens over centuries and is bound up with attitudes to mountain asceticism.

entities.name: Kappa
entities.role: The river child with a dish of water on its head
symbols: the water-filled dish on the crown
entities.abode: Rivers, ponds and irrigation channels
entities.bio: A green child-sized water spirit that drowns swimmers, loves cucumbers, and is defeated by being bowed to.
entities.longBio: The kappa is about the size of a child, green, with webbed hands, a beak, a shell, and a depression on top of its head holding water. It lives in rivers and drowns swimmers and horses, and folklore attributes a specific and unpleasant fixation to it involving the shirikodama, a mythical organ. It also has two weaknesses that are pure comedy. It is obsessively polite: if you bow to a kappa it must bow back, spilling the water from its head, at which point it is powerless until refilled. And it loves cucumbers above all things, which is why cucumber sushi rolls are called kappamaki, and why children were sent to throw a cucumber into the river before swimming.
entities.variantTraditions: Kappa lore was clearly serving as a practical warning to children about rivers; the drowning risk it encodes was entirely real.

entities.name: Oni
entities.role: The ogres of the northeast gate
entities.abode: Onigashima, the mountains, and the kimon gate
festivals: Setsubun, the bean-throwing at the start of spring
entities.bio: Horned, club-wielding ogres in tiger-skin, associated with the unlucky northeast and driven out with beans each spring.
entities.longBio: Oni are large, horned, red or blue, and carry an iron club - the phrase for an unstoppable advantage is oni with an iron club. Their appearance is derived from geomancy: the northeast is the kimon or demon gate, the unlucky quarter, and the northeast belongs to the ox and the tiger in the zodiac, so oni have ox horns and tiger-skin loincloths. Kyoto and Edo both had temples sited to guard the northeast approach. They cause plague, disaster and famine, eat people, and are the standard antagonist of folk tales. Every February at Setsubun households throw roasted soybeans out of the door shouting demons out, fortune in, which is among the most widely observed customs in Japan.
entities.variantTraditions: The Buddhist hell-wardens and the folk oni merged over time; the tiger-and-ox derivation of their appearance is well attested.

entities.name: Yuki-onna
entities.role: The snow woman
entities.abode: The mountains in winter
entities.bio: She spares a young woodcutter on condition he never speaks of her, marries him years later under another name, and leaves when he does.
entities.longBio: In Hearn's telling, two woodcutters are caught by a blizzard and shelter in a hut. The younger wakes to see a woman in white breathing on the older man, who dies of it; she turns to him, says he is too young and she pities him, and spares him on condition that he never tell anyone what he saw, or she will kill him. Years later he marries a beautiful woman named O-Yuki, who does not age, and they have ten children. One night by the lamp he remarks that she reminds him of something that happened long ago, and tells her. She rises, tells him she is that woman, and that only the children keep her from killing him - then dissolves into white mist and is gone through the smoke-hole.
entities.variantTraditions: Hearn says he had the story from a farmer in Musashi; earlier yuki-onna traditions vary widely and are often simply lethal, without the marriage.

entities.name: Tanuki
entities.role: The shape-shifting raccoon dog with a taste for mischief
entities.abode: The hills, and the doorway of every restaurant
entities.bio: A transforming trickster who turns leaves into money and drums on his own belly, and now stands outside bars in ceramic.
entities.longBio: Tanuki are shape-shifters like kitsune but with none of the menace: where the fox deceives for gain or revenge, the tanuki deceives for the fun of it, and usually comes off worse. They turn leaves into coins that revert, disguise themselves as monks or teapots, and drum on their bellies at night in the hills. The famous ceramic tanuki outside restaurants carries eight lucky attributes, including a straw hat against trouble, a sake flask for virtue, a promissory note for trust, and comically enlarged testicles for financial luck - the last derived from a pun on a phrase used by goldsmiths for a thin sheet of gold. The story of the tanuki that turned into a teakettle is among the best-loved in Japan.
entities.variantTraditions: The animal is a real species, Nyctereutes procyonoides, and is not a raccoon or a badger despite both being used in translation.
